---
title: "Elevation"
description: >
  Slope costs for walking and cycling from an elevation raster: the two
  cost functions, rasters in projected coordinate systems, voids, and
  results that do not depend on the machine.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
```

Walking and cycling uphill take longer. When the data directory has a
GeoTIFF elevation raster (`.tif`), `build_network()` samples it every 10 m
along each street, at the nearest pixel, and multiplies the street's
walking and cycling times by the average cost of its slopes. Car times do
not change.

This page uses the Porto Alegre sample of r5r 2.5.0, which has a raster of
the city (`poa_elevation.tif`, SRTM data at about 90 m).

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(peabiru)
poa <- r5r_sample(c("poa_osm.pbf", "poa_elevation.tif", "poa_hexgrid.csv"),
                  dir = file.path(tempdir(), "poa_elevation"))
hexes <- read.csv(file.path(poa, "poa_hexgrid.csv"))
pts <- hexes[seq(1, nrow(hexes), by = 40), ]
nrow(pts)
```

## Tobler and Minetti

`elevation` picks the cost function: `"TOBLER"` (the default, Tobler's
hiking function) or `"MINETTI"` (Minetti's energy cost of walking and
cycling); `"NONE"` ignores the raster.

```{r models}
flat <- build_network(poa, elevation = "NONE", n_threads = 2)
tobler <- build_network(poa, n_threads = 2)
minetti <- build_network(poa, elevation = "MINETTI", n_threads = 2)
tobler

walk <- function(net) {
  travel_time_matrix(net, pts, pts, mode = "WALK", max_trip_duration = 60,
                     n_threads = 2)
}
times <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = c("from_id", "to_id")),
                list(walk(flat), walk(tobler), walk(minetti)))
names(times)[3:5] <- c("none", "tobler", "minetti")
summary(times[3:5])
```

Pairs reached within the hour on flat ground can take longer than that with
the slopes, so the number of pairs within `max_trip_duration` changes too
(here, of the pairs reached in all three).

A raster also turns off one shortcut: without one, a walking matrix with
more origins than destinations is searched from the destinations; with a
raster, slopes make the trip one way differ from the trip back, and the
search runs from the origins.

## Rasters in other coordinate systems

The raster can be in WGS 84 longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326) or in one of
the projected and geographic systems used for Brazil and worldwide whose
transform is reproduced exactly: SIRGAS 2000 (EPSG:4674), SAD69, Córrego
Alegre and their UTM zones, SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic, WGS 84 / UTM
and WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator (the list is in `?build_network`). Here the
raster is warped with GDAL (through 'sf') to SIRGAS 2000 / UTM zone 22S
(EPSG:31982):

```{r utm, eval = requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE), message = FALSE}
utm <- file.path(tempdir(), "poa_utm")
dir.create(utm, showWarnings = FALSE)
invisible(file.copy(file.path(poa, "poa_osm.pbf"), utm))
sf::gdal_utils("warp", file.path(poa, "poa_elevation.tif"),
               file.path(utm, "poa_elevation_utm.tif"),
               options = c("-t_srs", "EPSG:31982", "-r", "near"))
tobler_utm <- build_network(utm, n_threads = 2)
both <- merge(walk(tobler), walk(tobler_utm), by = c("from_id", "to_id"))
summary(both$travel_time_p50.y - both$travel_time_p50.x)
```

The times change a little, because the pixels of the warped raster are not
those of the original.

In a projected system, which pixel a street point falls in is decided by
sines and cosines of the projection. For a point within nanometres of the
boundary between two pixels, the last bits of those functions decide, and
they differ between Java virtual machines and processors. peabiru
computes them as Java's `StrictMath` does, so a network gives the same
results on every machine, and warns with the number of such points when
there are any (about one in a hundred million for 30 m pixels).
Reprojecting the raster to EPSG:4326 removes the question.

## Voids and no-data values

Elevations are kept, as R5 keeps them, in decimetres in 16-bit integers, so
values beyond +/-3276.7 m wrap around: SRTM's voids (-32768) become 0 m,
a no-data value of -9999 becomes 3108.2 m, and a `NaN` no-data value 0 m.
peabiru stores them that way and warns, counting them. The raster below is
a small synthetic one over the São Paulo sample, with a few voids:

```{r voids}
voids <- file.path(tempdir(), "spo_voids")
dir.create(voids, showWarnings = FALSE)
invisible(file.copy(file.path(data_path, c("spo_osm.pbf", "spo_gtfs.zip")), voids))
invisible(file.copy(file.path("..", "..", "tests", "testthat", "fixtures", "spo_voids.tif"), voids))
spo_voids <- build_network(voids, n_threads = 2)
```

Fill the voids (for instance with `gdal_fillnodata`) before building the
network to avoid them.

## Scenarios

A routing call with a scenario of car speeds or traffic stress
(`new_carspeeds`, `carspeed_scale`, `new_lts`; see
[Scenarios](scenarios.html)) routes without the slope costs, and says so:

```{r scenario}
x <- travel_time_matrix(tobler, pts[1:3, ], pts[1:3, ], mode = "WALK",
                        carspeed_scale = 0.8, n_threads = 2)
```
